name: Thirumetrali Nathar Temple, Kanchipuram
deity: Shiva as Thirumetrali Nathar (Metraleeswarar), the west-facing lingam, with Odha-Urugeesar and the goddess Kamakshi (Parasakthi)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, sung in the Tevaram by Appar and Sundarar (7th–8th century)
summary: In the Pillaiyarpalayam quarter of Kanchipuram, the west-facing Thirumetrali Nathar shares his temple with Odha-Urugeesar, the lingam that tradition says melted into being at the sound of Sambandar's song.

sections.history: Thirumetrali, the Tirukkachi Metrali of the hymns, is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and a Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, the old northern country whose capital was Kanchipuram. Appar and Sundarar each sang a pathigam to the Lord here, which places the shrine among the city's sacred sites by the seventh century. The temple stands on Thirumetrali Street in Pillaiyarpalayam, the weavers' quarter of the city, about a kilometre from the bus stand and not far from the Vegavathi river. Its name is read as the shrine that faces west — merku in Tamil — for the lingam of Thirumetrali Nathar looks westward, unlike most sanctums. Today it is administered by the Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Department of Tamil Nadu.
sections.architecture: The temple is a modest walled complex in the Dravidian manner, unusual in having two principal lingams. The west-facing sanctum of Thirumetrali Nathar is the older focus of worship, while the rajagopuram and main entrance line up instead with the shrine of Odha-Urugeesar, before which sits the Nandi that receives the Pradosham worship. The goddess has her own east-facing shrine. The image of Odha-Urugeesar is known for the feet that tradition says remain visible at the base of the lingam.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that Vishnu longed to take on the form of a lingam and prayed to Shiva, who bade him worship the west-facing, self-manifested lingam here. Vishnu sat in penance on the bank of the Vegavathi, and when the child-saint Sambandar, passing on pilgrimage, sang from a distance, the hymn so moved him that he melted into a lingam, his feet alone left visible — hence Odha-Urugeesar, the Lord who melted at the song. Another telling says it was Shiva himself who, charmed by Sambandar, turned westward to listen.
sections.festivals: Pradosham, kept twice a month before the Nandi facing Odha-Urugeesar, is the most distinctive observance here. Maha Shivaratri, Karthigai Deepam and the Arudra Darshan of Margazhi are kept with special worship, alongside the festivals of the goddess; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Thirumetrali is a neighbourhood temple among the silk-weaving lanes of Kanchipuram, quieter than the great shrines nearby. Visitors pause before both lingams — the west-facing Lord and the melted one with his feet — and remember Sambandar's song. It is easily combined in a day with Ekambareswarar, Kamakshi, Kailasanathar and the city's other Tevaram shrines.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most neighbourhood temples of Kanchipuram. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is on Thirumetrali Street in Pillaiyarpalayam, Kanchipuram, about 1 km from the Kanchipuram bus stand and a short auto ride from the railway station. Kanchipuram is linked by road to Chennai, Chengalpattu, Vellore and Arakkonam; Chennai International Airport, roughly 70 km away, is the nearest airport.
